sql-basics:0.prompt: A migration file contains CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN and DROP VIEW statements. Which SQL sublanguage do all three belong to?
options: DML (data manipulation)
DDL (data definition)
DCL (data control)
TCL (transaction control)
sql-basics:0.explanation: All three change schema objects (indexes, tables, views), which is DDL. DML would be statements that read or change rows (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE), which none of these do.

sql-basics:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL you run the statements below. What is the state of the orders table afterwards?
options: The note column exists, because DDL auto-commits the open transaction
The statement errors, because DDL is not allowed inside a transaction block
The note column does not exist, because PostgreSQL DDL is transactional
The note column exists but is hidden until the next VACUUM runs
sql-basics:0.explanation: PostgreSQL supports transactional DDL, so the ROLLBACK undoes the ALTER TABLE. The auto-commit behaviour is true of MySQL and Oracle, which is why that distractor is tempting, but it does not apply to PostgreSQL.

sql-basics:0.prompt: Which of these statements is DCL (data control language)?
options: COMMIT;
TRUNCATE audit_log;
GRANT SELECT ON orders TO reporting;
SAVEPOINT before_import;
sql-basics:0.explanation: GRANT and REVOKE manage privileges, which is DCL. COMMIT and SAVEPOINT are transaction control (TCL), and TRUNCATE is classified as DDL even though it removes data.

sql-basics:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which rows are in table t after this script completes?
options: Rows 'a' and 'c'
Rows 'a', 'b' and 'c'
Only row 'c'
No rows, because the rollback cancels the whole transaction
sql-basics:0.explanation: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes only the work done after s1 (inserting 'b') and keeps the transaction open, so 'a' and 'c' are committed. A plain ROLLBACK would discard everything, but rolling back to a savepoint does not.

sql-basics:0.prompt: Your migration tool wraps every migration in a single transaction. Which PostgreSQL statement will fail with "cannot run inside a transaction block"?
options: TRUNCATE sessions;
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
CREATE TABLE audit (id bigint PRIMARY KEY);
sql-basics:0.explanation: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY needs several transactions internally so it cannot run inside an explicit transaction block. TRUNCATE, ALTER TABLE and CREATE TABLE are all transactional in PostgreSQL and run fine inside BEGIN/COMMIT.

sql-basics:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what is a real difference between DELETE FROM sessions (no WHERE) and TRUNCATE sessions?
options: TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back, while DELETE can
TRUNCATE skips per-row ON DELETE triggers and frees the storage immediately
TRUNCATE ignores foreign keys from other tables that reference sessions
DELETE without a WHERE clause is treated as DDL and auto-commits
sql-basics:0.explanation: TRUNCATE drops the table's data files instead of deleting row by row, so row-level ON DELETE triggers do not fire and space is reclaimed at once. It is still transactional in PostgreSQL, and it errors on referencing foreign keys unless you add CASCADE.

sql-basics:0.prompt: Your Node API connects as role app_rw. It must read and write rows in orders but never change the schema. Which setup follows least privilege in PostgreSQL?
options: Make app_rw the owner of orders so it never hits permission errors
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE shop TO app_rw
GRANT USAGE on the schema, then SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on orders; a separate migration role owns the table
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO app_rw and nothing else
sql-basics:0.explanation: Table owners can ALTER and DROP the table, so the app role should hold only DML privileges, plus USAGE on the schema so it can find the table. Database-level ALL covers only CONNECT, CREATE and TEMP, not table access, and USAGE alone lets the role see the table but not read it.

sql-basics:0.prompt: Which of these are TCL (transaction control) statements? Select all that apply.
options: COMMIT
ROLLBACK
SAVEPOINT
GRANT
TRUNCATE
sql-basics:0.explanation: COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT control transaction boundaries. GRANT is DCL (privileges) and TRUNCATE is DDL, even though both change what a session can see.

sql-basics:0.prompt: You run schema migrations against PostgreSQL 16 inside explicit transactions. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: If one statement in the migration fails, none of its earlier schema changes are left behind
Locks taken by ALTER TABLE are held until the transaction ends, so a long migration can block application queries
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can be part of the same transaction as other DDL
Each DDL statement implicitly commits whatever came before it in the transaction
sql-basics:0.explanation: Transactional DDL means a failed migration rolls back cleanly, but ALTER TABLE's ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock lasts until COMMIT, so long transactions are risky. CONCURRENTLY cannot run in a transaction block, and implicit commits are MySQL/Oracle behaviour, not PostgreSQL.

sql-basics:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a TRUNCATE executed inside a transaction can be undone with ROLLBACK.
options: True
False
sql-basics:0.explanation: TRUNCATE is transaction-safe in PostgreSQL: the old data files are kept until the transaction commits, so a ROLLBACK restores the rows. Many people assume otherwise because TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back in some other databases.

sql-basics:0.prompt: REVOKE is a TCL statement because it undoes an earlier change.
options: True
False
sql-basics:0.explanation: REVOKE removes privileges previously granted, so it is DCL alongside GRANT. TCL statements (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT) control transaction boundaries, not permissions.

sql-basics:1.prompt: Why does this PostgreSQL query fail with "column total does not exist"?
options: Aliases need double quotes before they can be referenced
WHERE is evaluated before the SELECT list, so the alias does not exist yet
Arithmetic expressions cannot be compared in WHERE
The alias conflicts with a built-in aggregate called total
sql-basics:1.explanation: Logically FROM and WHERE run before SELECT computes output columns, so WHERE cannot see the alias. Repeat the expression (WHERE price * qty > 100) or wrap it in a subquery; quoting the alias does not change the evaluation order.

sql-basics:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, in which clause can you reference a SELECT-list alias such as total?
options: WHERE
HAVING
ORDER BY
a JOIN's ON condition
sql-basics:1.explanation: ORDER BY runs after the SELECT list is computed, so output aliases are visible there. WHERE, ON and HAVING are evaluated before output columns exist, so in PostgreSQL they must repeat the expression.

sql-basics:1.prompt: A feed endpoint pages with SELECT * FROM posts LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40. Users sometimes see the same post on two pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: OFFSET is applied before WHERE, so it skips the wrong rows
There is no ORDER BY, so PostgreSQL may return rows in a different order on each query
LIMIT is not supported together with OFFSET in PostgreSQL
The posts table needs a VACUUM before OFFSET gives stable results
sql-basics:1.explanation: Without ORDER BY, SQL guarantees no order, and the plan or physical layout can change between requests, so pages overlap or skip rows. VACUUM may change physical order but is not a fix; only a deterministic ORDER BY is.

sql-basics:1.prompt: The feed now uses ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20, but many posts share the same created_at and pages still repeat rows. What is the right fix?
options: Switch to ORDER BY created_at ASC
Add a unique tiebreaker: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
Add DISTINCT to the SELECT
Create a non-unique index on created_at
sql-basics:1.explanation: Rows tied on created_at can come back in any order, so the cut between pages is nondeterministic. A unique tiebreaker such as id makes the order total. An index may speed up the sort but does not make ties deterministic.

sql-basics:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY last_login DESC puts users who never logged in (last_login IS NULL) at the top. How do you push them to the bottom?
options: ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS LAST
ORDER BY COALESCE(last_login, 0) DESC
WHERE last_login IS NOT NULL ORDER BY last_login DESC
ORDER BY last_login DESC NULLS FIRST
sql-basics:1.explanation: PostgreSQL sorts NULL as larger than any value, so DESC puts NULLs first by default; NULLS LAST overrides that. Filtering with IS NOT NULL removes those users entirely, and COALESCE with 0 fails on a timestamp column.

sql-basics:1.prompt: An admin page uses ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET 500000 and is slow even with an index on id. Why, and what is the usual fix?
options: OFFSET disables index use; add a hint to force the index
PostgreSQL still produces and discards the 500,000 skipped rows; use keyset pagination such as WHERE id > $lastId ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
LIMIT is applied before ORDER BY, so the whole table is sorted; move LIMIT into a subquery
Large OFFSET values overflow an int; cast the offset to bigint
sql-basics:1.explanation: OFFSET n means the executor must walk n rows before returning anything, so cost grows with page depth. Keyset pagination seeks straight to the last seen key using the index. PostgreSQL has no index hints, and LIMIT is applied after ORDER BY.

sql-basics:1.prompt: Which rows does this PostgreSQL query return?
sql-basics:1.code:
SELECT * FROM accounts
WHERE status = 'active' OR status = 'trial' AND plan = 'pro';
options: Active or trial accounts, but only on the pro plan
All active accounts, plus trial accounts on the pro plan
Only accounts that are both active and on the pro plan
No rows, because status cannot equal two values at once
sql-basics:1.explanation: AND binds tighter than OR, so this reads as status = 'active' OR (status = 'trial' AND plan = 'pro'). To restrict both statuses to pro, write (status = 'active' OR status = 'trial') AND plan = 'pro', or use status IN (...).

sql-basics:1.prompt: orders has a B-tree index on created_at (timestamptz). Which WHERE predicates can use that index directly? Select all that apply.
options: created_at BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-02-01'
date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-01-15'
created_at + interval '1 day' > now()
sql-basics:1.explanation: A plain index on a column helps when the column appears bare on one side of a comparison. Wrapping it in a function or arithmetic hides it from the index; rewrite as a range on created_at or build an expression index.

sql-basics:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which predicates return rows with price from 10 to 20 inclusive? Select all that apply.
options: price BETWEEN 10 AND 20
price >= 10 AND price <= 20
price > 10 AND price < 20
price BETWEEN 20 AND 10
sql-basics:1.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends and means low <= x AND x <= high. Writing the bounds in reverse order matches nothing (BETWEEN SYMMETRIC would accept that), and strict > and < leave out 10 and 20.

sql-basics:1.prompt: Without ORDER BY, PostgreSQL returns rows in the order they were inserted.
options: True
False
sql-basics:1.explanation: Without ORDER BY the order is unspecified. Updates, VACUUM, parallel scans, synchronized scans and plan changes can all change it, so insertion order often appears in small tests but is never guaranteed.

sql-basics:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, SELECT DISTINCT ON (customer_id) * FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id, created_at DESC returns each customer's most recent order.
options: True
False
sql-basics:1.explanation: DISTINCT ON keeps the first row of each group in ORDER BY order, and the ORDER BY must start with the DISTINCT ON expressions. Sorting created_at DESC inside each customer makes the latest order the first row kept.

sql-basics:2.prompt: customers has 3 rows (A, B, C). orders has 2 rows for A and 1 row for B. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id return?
sql-basics:2.explanation: A matches 2 orders (2 rows), B matches 1 (1 row), and C has no match but is kept with NULL order columns (1 row): 4 in total. Answering 3 assumes one row per customer, which only holds if each customer has at most one order.

sql-basics:2.prompt: This query should list every customer with their paid orders, including customers with none. Customers without paid orders are missing. Why?
sql-basics:2.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
options: LEFT JOIN cannot be combined with WHERE
The WHERE filter discards the NULL-extended rows, turning it into an inner join; move the condition into the ON clause
status needs an index for the LEFT JOIN to keep unmatched rows
The join condition is reversed; it should be c.id = o.customer_id
sql-basics:2.explanation: For unmatched customers o.status is NULL, and NULL = 'paid' is not true, so WHERE removes them. Putting AND o.status = 'paid' in ON filters which orders match while still keeping every customer. The order of operands in the ON equality makes no difference.

sql-basics:2.prompt: sizes has 5 rows and colors has 8 rows. How many rows does SELECT * FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colors return?
sql-basics:2.explanation: A CROSS JOIN is the Cartesian product: every size paired with every color, 5 x 8 = 40. 13 would be a UNION ALL of the two tables, not a join.

sql-basics:2.prompt: employees(id, name, manager_id) where the CEO has manager_id NULL. Which query lists every employee with their manager's name, including the CEO?
options: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.id = m.manager_id
SELECT e.name, m.name FROM employees e CROSS JOIN employees m WHERE e.manager_id = m.id
sql-basics:2.explanation: A self LEFT JOIN on e.manager_id = m.id keeps the CEO with a NULL manager name. The inner join and the CROSS JOIN + WHERE drop the CEO. Reversing the condition finds each employee's direct reports instead of their manager.

sql-basics:2.prompt: This report shows revenue far too high for customers whose orders have several items. What is the cause?
sql-basics:2.code:
SELECT c.id, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue, COUNT(oi.id) AS items
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id;
options: SUM ignores NULLs, which inflates the total
Each order row is repeated once per item before grouping, so o.amount is summed several times
GROUP BY c.id must also include o.id for SUM to be correct
COUNT(oi.id) and SUM(o.amount) cannot appear in the same SELECT
sql-basics:2.explanation: Joining one-to-many twice fans out rows: an order with 3 items appears 3 times, so its amount is counted 3 times. Aggregate items per order in a subquery (or use separate subqueries) before joining. Adding o.id to GROUP BY changes the grain but does not give per-customer revenue.

sql-basics:2.prompt: You reconcile ledger(txn_id) against bank_feed(txn_id) and need every transaction that is missing from either side, in one query. Which join fits?
options: ledger INNER JOIN bank_feed USING (txn_id)
ledger LEFT JOIN bank_feed USING (txn_id) WHERE bank_feed.txn_id IS NULL
ledger FULL OUTER JOIN bank_feed ON ledger.txn_id = bank_feed.txn_id WHERE ledger.txn_id IS NULL OR bank_feed.txn_id IS NULL
ledger CROSS JOIN bank_feed WHERE ledger.txn_id <> bank_feed.txn_id
sql-basics:2.explanation: A FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides, and the IS NULL checks keep only the mismatches. The LEFT JOIN version finds only ledger rows missing from the bank feed, not the reverse. The CROSS JOIN with <> returns almost every pair.

sql-basics:2.prompt: Which query returns the same rows as orders o RIGHT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id (ignoring column order)?
options: customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
orders o FULL JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
sql-basics:2.explanation: A RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table, so swapping the table order and using LEFT JOIN is equivalent. Keeping orders on the left with LEFT JOIN would preserve all orders instead of all customers.

sql-basics:2.prompt: customers.id is a primary key. Which queries return each customer with at least one order exactly once? Select all that apply.
options: SELECT c.* FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)
SELECT DISTINCT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
sql-basics:2.explanation: EXISTS is a semi-join that never duplicates outer rows, and DISTINCT removes join duplicates (safe because id is unique). The plain inner join repeats a customer once per order, and the LEFT JOIN also includes customers with no orders.

sql-basics:2.prompt: Which statements about join conditions in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: For an INNER JOIN, putting a filter in ON or in WHERE gives the same result
For a LEFT JOIN, a filter on the right table in ON keeps unmatched left rows, while the same filter in WHERE removes them
NATURAL JOIN matches on every column with the same name, so adding updated_at to both tables can silently change the results
JOIN ... USING (customer_id) outputs customer_id twice, once per table
CROSS JOIN requires an ON clause
sql-basics:2.explanation: Inner joins are commutative with respect to filters, but outer joins are not. NATURAL JOIN is fragile because its join columns depend on the schema. USING outputs one merged column, and CROSS JOIN takes no ON clause at all.

sql-basics:2.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a self join needs a table alias for at least one copy, because the same table name cannot appear twice in FROM without one.
options: True
False
sql-basics:2.explanation: Without aliases PostgreSQL raises "table name specified more than once", and column references would be ambiguous anyway. Aliases such as e and m tell the two roles apart.

sql-basics:2.prompt: An INNER JOIN between a 1,000-row table and a 10-row table can never return more than 1,000 rows.
options: True
False
sql-basics:2.explanation: If the join key is not unique on either side (many-to-many), each row can match many rows, up to 1,000 x 10 = 10,000. The 1,000 cap only holds when every left row matches at most one right row.

sql-basics:3.prompt: You need departments whose average salary is above 100,000. Which query is correct?
options: SELECT dept_id FROM employees WHERE AVG(salary) > 100000 GROUP BY dept_id
SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 100000
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS a FROM employees WHERE a > 100000 GROUP BY dept_id
SELECT dept_id FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id, AVG(salary) > 100000
sql-basics:3.explanation: WHERE filters rows before grouping, so it cannot use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Aggregates in WHERE are an error, and so is referencing the alias a there.

sql-basics:3.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL reject this query?
options: COUNT(*) cannot be used together with GROUP BY
name is neither grouped nor aggregated, so there is no single value for it per department
GROUP BY columns must appear last in the SELECT list
dept_id must be wrapped in an aggregate such as MAX
sql-basics:3.explanation: Each output row is a department, but one department has many names, so PostgreSQL errors with "must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function". MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY off would pick an arbitrary name, which is the habit this error prevents.

sql-basics:3.prompt: e.id is the primary key of employees. Does this run in PostgreSQL 16?
sql-basics:3.code:
SELECT e.id, e.name, e.email, COUNT(o.id)
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.sales_rep_id = e.id
GROUP BY e.id;
options: No: name and email must be listed in GROUP BY
Yes: other columns of e are functionally dependent on its primary key, so they may be selected
Yes, but name and email come from an arbitrary row in each group
No: LEFT JOIN cannot be combined with GROUP BY
sql-basics:3.explanation: Since 9.1, PostgreSQL allows ungrouped columns of a table when that table's primary key is in GROUP BY, because they are determined by it. The values are not arbitrary; there is only one possible value per group.

sql-basics:3.prompt: Column v holds the values 1, 1, NULL, 2. What do COUNT(*), COUNT(v) and COUNT(DISTINCT v) return?
sql-basics:3.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows (4). COUNT(v) skips NULL (3). COUNT(DISTINCT v) counts distinct non-NULL values {1, 2} (2). Answering 3 for the last one wrongly treats NULL as a distinct value.

sql-basics:3.prompt: scores has three rows: 10, NULL, 20. What does SELECT AVG(score) FROM scores return?
options: NULL
An error, because the column contains a NULL
sql-basics:3.explanation: AVG ignores NULL inputs, so it computes (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. To treat missing scores as 0 you would write AVG(COALESCE(score, 0)), which gives 10.

sql-basics:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, you want daily paid and refunded counts from payments in a single pass. Which expression correctly counts paid rows?
options: COUNT(status = 'paid') AS paid
COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid
SUM(status = 'paid') AS paid
COUNT(*) WHERE status = 'paid' AS paid
sql-basics:3.explanation: The FILTER clause restricts which rows reach that aggregate. COUNT(status = 'paid') counts every non-NULL boolean, true or false, so it counts nearly all rows. SUM over a boolean has no PostgreSQL overload, and WHERE cannot follow an aggregate like that.

sql-basics:3.prompt: Customer 999 has no orders. What does SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 999 return?
options: Zero rows
One row containing 0
One row containing NULL
An error, because there is nothing to sum
sql-basics:3.explanation: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, and SUM over no input is NULL (COUNT would be 0). Use COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0) if the API must return 0.

sql-basics:3.prompt: Which of these aggregates skip NULL input values? Select all that apply.
options: COUNT(*)
COUNT(email)
AVG(score)
MAX(score)
sql-basics:3.explanation: Aggregates over an expression ignore NULL inputs, so COUNT(email), AVG and MAX skip NULLs. COUNT(*) counts rows, not values, so rows that are entirely NULL still count.

sql-basics:3.prompt: Which groupings does GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, product) produce? Select all that apply.
options: (region, product)
(region)
() — the grand total
(product)
sql-basics:3.explanation: ROLLUP produces hierarchical prefixes: (region, product), (region) and (). A per-product subtotal across regions needs CUBE or an explicit GROUPING SETS entry.

sql-basics:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, HAVING can be used without GROUP BY; the whole result set is then treated as a single group.
options: True
False
sql-basics:3.explanation: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 is valid: with no GROUP BY there is one implicit group, and HAVING decides whether that single row is returned.

sql-basics:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, GROUP BY guarantees that the output is sorted by the grouping columns.
options: True
False
sql-basics:3.explanation: The planner often uses HashAggregate, which returns groups in no particular order. Sorted output with a GroupAggregate plan is a side effect, so add ORDER BY when order matters.

sql-basics:4.prompt: SELECT * FROM coupons WHERE discount = NULL returns no rows, even though some discounts are NULL. Why?
options: NULL values are not stored in indexed columns
Comparing anything with = NULL yields NULL (unknown), which WHERE treats as not true; use discount IS NULL
The literal NULL must be quoted as 'NULL'
PostgreSQL requires a cast such as NULL::numeric before comparing
sql-basics:4.explanation: NULL means unknown, so = NULL is never true, even for NULL rows. IS NULL is the predicate that tests for NULL. Quoting it compares against the four-letter string 'NULL', and a cast does not change the logic.

sql-basics:4.prompt: orders.customer_id is nullable, and one order has customer_id NULL. What does this query return?
sql-basics:4.code:
SELECT id FROM customers
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
options: Customers without orders, as intended
No rows at all
Every customer
An error, because the subquery contains NULL
sql-basics:4.explanation: x NOT IN (..., NULL) evaluates to NULL whenever x matches none of the other values, so no row ever passes. Use NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL anti-join, which behave as expected with NULLs.

sql-basics:4.prompt: tickets.status is nullable. WHERE status <> 'cancelled' also drops tickets whose status is NULL. Which predicate keeps them?
options: status != 'cancelled'
status IS DISTINCT FROM 'cancelled'
NOT (status = 'cancelled')
status NOT IN ('cancelled')
sql-basics:4.explanation: IS DISTINCT FROM treats NULL as an ordinary comparable value, so NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 'cancelled' is true. The other three forms all evaluate to NULL for NULL status and filter those rows out.

sql-basics:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, first_name = 'Ada', middle_name = NULL, last_name = 'Lovelace'. Which expression returns 'Ada Lovelace'?
options: first_name || ' ' || middle_name || ' ' || last_name
concat_ws(' ', first_name, middle_name, last_name)
concat(first_name, ' ', middle_name, ' ', last_name)
COALESCE(first_name || middle_name || last_name, '')
sql-basics:4.explanation: concat_ws skips NULL arguments and puts the separator only between non-NULL values. The || operator returns NULL if any operand is NULL, and concat treats NULL as an empty string but keeps both spaces ('Ada  Lovelace').

sql-basics:4.prompt: Under SQL three-valued logic, which expression evaluates to FALSE?
options: NULL OR FALSE
NULL = NULL
NULL AND FALSE
NOT NULL
sql-basics:4.explanation: FALSE AND anything is FALSE, whatever the unknown value is. NULL OR FALSE depends on the unknown, so it is NULL. NULL = NULL and NOT NULL are also NULL.

sql-basics:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL 16, UNIQUE (tenant_id, email) still allows duplicate emails for rows where tenant_id IS NULL. How do you prevent that?
options: Add a CHECK (email IS NOT NULL) constraint
Declare the constraint as UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (tenant_id, email)
Recreate the index as a hash index
Wrap the columns in UNIQUE (COALESCE(tenant_id), email)
sql-basics:4.explanation: By default, unique constraints treat NULLs as distinct, so rows with a NULL tenant_id never conflict. PostgreSQL 15+ supports NULLS NOT DISTINCT to treat NULLs as equal (a unique index on COALESCE(tenant_id, 0) is the older workaround). A CHECK on email does nothing about the NULL tenant.

sql-basics:4.prompt: A metrics query computes revenue / order_count and crashes with "division by zero" for days with no orders. What is the idiomatic PostgreSQL fix if you want NULL for those days?
options: revenue / COALESCE(order_count, 0)
revenue / NULLIF(order_count, 0)
revenue / (order_count IS NOT NULL)
COALESCE(revenue / order_count, 0)
sql-basics:4.explanation: NULLIF(order_count, 0) turns 0 into NULL, and division by NULL returns NULL instead of raising an error. COALESCE(order_count, 0) still divides by zero, and wrapping the division in COALESCE does not help because the error is raised first.

sql-basics:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which expressions evaluate to TRUE? Select all that apply.
options: NULL IS NULL
NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL
NULL = NULL
1 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL
NULL <> 1
sql-basics:4.explanation: IS NULL and IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM are null-safe and always return true or false. Ordinary comparisons such as = and <> with a NULL operand return NULL, not TRUE.

sql-basics:4.prompt: Which SQL operations treat all NULLs as equal to each other? Select all that apply.
options: GROUP BY puts all NULL keys into a single group
SELECT DISTINCT collapses repeated NULLs into one row
A join ON a.x = b.x matches a NULL to a NULL
UNION removes rows that are duplicates, including rows with NULL in the same columns
sql-basics:4.explanation: Grouping, DISTINCT and set operations use "not distinct" semantics, so NULLs count as duplicates. Join conditions use ordinary =, where NULL = NULL is unknown, so NULL keys never match.

sql-basics:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, CHECK (price > 0) rejects a row where price is NULL.
options: True
False
sql-basics:4.explanation: A CHECK constraint fails only when its expression is FALSE; NULL > 0 is NULL, so the row is accepted. Add NOT NULL if missing prices must be rejected.

sql-basics:4.prompt: After a LEFT JOIN, a NULL in the right table's primary-key column reliably shows that the left row had no match.
options: True
False
sql-basics:4.explanation: A primary key can never be NULL in stored rows, so a NULL there must come from NULL-extension of an unmatched row. Testing a nullable non-key column would be unreliable, because a matched row could legitimately hold NULL.

sql-basics:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ($1) ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING fails with "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification". What is missing?
options: A primary key on users.id
A unique constraint or unique index on users.email
A RETURNING clause
An explicit BEGIN/COMMIT around the insert
sql-basics:5.explanation: ON CONFLICT (email) needs a unique index or constraint on exactly that column to detect conflicts. A primary key on id does not cover email, and transactions or RETURNING are unrelated to conflict detection.

sql-basics:5.prompt: In this PostgreSQL upsert, what does EXCLUDED.views refer to?
options: The value already stored in the existing row
The value from the row that was proposed for insertion (here 1)
The number of rows that conflicted
The views value from before the last UPDATE
sql-basics:5.explanation: EXCLUDED is the row that would have been inserted; the existing row is referenced by the table name (page_views.views). So this adds 1 to the stored count.

sql-basics:5.prompt: A Node handler does SELECT by email and then INSERT if no row was found. Under load you get unique-violation errors. Why does INSERT ... ON CONFLICT fix this?
options: It runs at SERIALIZABLE isolation automatically
It checks and inserts atomically, so two concurrent requests cannot both pass the existence check
It disables the unique index while the statement runs
It retries the SELECT until no conflicting row is found
sql-basics:5.explanation: With check-then-insert, two requests can both see no row and both insert. ON CONFLICT resolves the conflict inside one statement using the unique index, with no window between the check and the insert. It does not change the isolation level.

sql-basics:5.prompt: After inserting an order whose id is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, how does a Node service get the new id in the same round trip in PostgreSQL?
options: Call SELECT MAX(id) FROM orders right after the insert
Append RETURNING id to the INSERT
Read the id from the driver's rowCount
Run SELECT lastval() in a separate request without a transaction
sql-basics:5.explanation: RETURNING sends back columns of the inserted rows, including generated ids, in one statement. MAX(id) races with concurrent inserts, and rowCount is only the number of affected rows.

sql-basics:5.prompt: staging has two rows for SKU 'X1' with different prices. What happens to product X1 in PostgreSQL?
sql-basics:5.code:
UPDATE products p
SET price = s.price
FROM staging s
WHERE s.sku = p.sku;
options: The statement fails because a row would be updated twice
X1 is updated once, using one of the two staging prices, and which one is unpredictable
X1 is updated twice and ends with the last price in staging order
X1 gets the average of the two prices
sql-basics:5.explanation: PostgreSQL docs warn that when the FROM join yields several matches for a target row, only one is used to update it, and which one is not predictable. De-duplicate staging first, for example with DISTINCT ON. The "affect row a second time" error belongs to ON CONFLICT and MERGE.

sql-basics:5.prompt: You must purge 50 million expired rows from a busy PostgreSQL events table. What is the safest approach?
options: One DELETE ... WHERE expires_at < now() so it is atomic
Delete in batches (for example 10,000 rows by primary-key range per transaction) and let autovacuum keep up
TRUNCATE the table during peak traffic
UPDATE the rows to NULL first, then DELETE them
sql-basics:5.explanation: A single huge DELETE holds row locks and a long transaction, generates a burst of WAL and replication lag, and stops VACUUM from cleaning up until it ends. Batching keeps each transaction short. TRUNCATE would remove the rows you want to keep.

sql-basics:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what happens when you run this statement?
sql-basics:5.code:
INSERT INTO kv (k, v) VALUES ('a', 1), ('a', 2)
ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE SET v = EXCLUDED.v;
options: kv ends with ('a', 2), the last value wins
kv ends with ('a', 1), the first value wins
Error: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
Both rows are inserted because the conflict check runs after the statement
sql-basics:5.explanation: A single INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE may not update the same row twice, so duplicate keys within one batch raise an error. De-duplicate the input (for example in the Node layer or with DISTINCT ON) before upserting.

sql-basics:5.prompt: Which statements about RETURNING in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: It works with INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
It returns values filled in by column defaults, such as a generated id or created_at
With ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, rows that were skipped are not returned
It only works with single-row statements
sql-basics:5.explanation: RETURNING reports the final stored rows for all three DML commands, including defaults, and works for multi-row statements. Rows skipped by DO NOTHING are not returned, which surprises people who expect the existing row back.

sql-basics:5.prompt: orders.customer_id references customers(id). Which statements are true in PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: With ON DELETE CASCADE, deleting a customer also deletes their orders
With the default (NO ACTION), deleting a customer who still has orders fails
ON DELETE SET NULL works even if orders.customer_id is declared NOT NULL
PostgreSQL automatically creates an index on orders.customer_id for the foreign key
sql-basics:5.explanation: CASCADE propagates the delete, and NO ACTION rejects it while children exist. SET NULL would violate NOT NULL and fail. PostgreSQL indexes only the referenced key, not the referencing column, so add that index yourself or deletes and joins will scan orders.

sql-basics:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING without a conflict target skips rows that would violate any unique constraint on the table.
options: True
False
sql-basics:5.explanation: For DO NOTHING the conflict target is optional; leaving it out handles conflicts against any unique or exclusion constraint. DO UPDATE, by contrast, requires a conflict target.

sql-basics:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, UPDATE rewrites rows in place, so updating every row of a table does not increase its on-disk size.
options: True
False
sql-basics:5.explanation: Under MVCC, an UPDATE writes a new row version and marks the old one dead, so a full-table update can roughly double the table until VACUUM reclaims space. HOT updates reuse space within a page but only when there is room and no indexed column changes.
